en: A Commentary on the *Sūtra of Visualizing the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* by the Disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts, Peng Jiqing.
In explaining this sūtra, it is briefly divided into four parts: first, the title; second, the introductory section; third, the main body of the teaching; and fourth, the concluding section.

General Explanation. First, regarding the interpretation of the title: the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is fundamentally without differentiation; yet, in response to conditions and karmic resonance, it manifests in many ways.

This single gate of "Contemplating the Buddha" speaks to its fundamental essence: the Buddha is the virtue of nature (*xingde*), while contemplation is the virtue of cultivation (*xiude*). By means of nature, cultivation is subsumed.
Cultivation is entirely cultivation of this nature. Self and other are both quiescent; it is the single true mind that cuts off the ten directions and transcends them utterly.

All Mahāyāna sūtras extensively explain this point. This sūtra, by means of the title "Contemplation of Immeasurable Life," specifically clarifies the adornments of the environment and inhabitants of the Buddha of Ultimate Bliss, as well as his compassionate skillful means, distinguishing them from those of the Buddhas of other lands.
Excessive. Desiring to cause sentient beings to single-mindedly dedicate their merit so as to swiftly transcend birth and death, there are many gates of contemplation;

according to the capacities of those encountered—whether sharp or dull—they are all subsumed within the One Buddha, leaving none unencompassed. Though divided into nine grades, the myriad streams flow together toward the same destination.

Without departing from the bodies of retribution and transformation, one suddenly penetrates the Dharma-body; without going beyond the Shared Residence [heaven], one directly ascends to the stage of the "Successor to Buddhahood. Such expedient means are...
Peerless and incomparable. Those who encounter this sutra should truly give rise to a resolute mind and firmly shoulder their aspirations;
throughout this present physical existence, they shall swiftly be reborn in that land.
Second, regarding the explanation of the introductory section: from "Thus have I heard" up to "the place of pure karma" is termed the introductory section.
As for the fact that the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is about to be opened by using Vaidehī as the starting point:
it is because all sentient beings, relying upon ignorance, possess craving; relying upon craving, they engage in strife; this is solely due to their failure to realize that their own nature is empty.
In stillness, one falsely clings to the notions of self and person, deeming them to be truly existent. Thus, enmity and favor revolve like a turning waterwheel;

even were the Great Awakened One to manifest before one, it would be difficult to reverse fixed karma. It depends solely upon the individual’s single thought of recognizing their error, whereby all entanglements will naturally be liberated.
From this point, to initiate practice, purify Buddha-lands, and bring sentient beings to maturity is not beyond one's capacity. Therefore, know that this is the cause for entering the Way.
As for the conditions: one must first discern and shatter the flowers in the sky, and feel a profound sense of urgency regarding birth and death;
only then can one give rise to the supramundane mind. Once the supramundane mind has arisen, one can then seek rebirth in the land of no-desire.

Knowing how to seek rebirth in the land of no-desire, one can then suddenly cease worldly toil and cultivate various pure deeds. When these pure deeds are perfected, the Sahā world is transformed into the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Attaining birth in the highest grade, hearing the Dharma and realizing its fruit, and simultaneously liberating karmic enemies and relatives across kalpas—is this not the deed of a great man?
Nevertheless, there are briefly two types of sentient beings in the world who are unwilling to resolve their minds [for enlightenment].

The first is those who cling to existence, asserting that the various phenomena before their eyes truly exist, and who falsely give rise to attachment for gain, offerings, fame, and reputation. This...
Great ignorance is truly not worth censuring. Those who are confined by the teachings of names and forms reckon birth and extinction to be the true and eternal;

those who aspire to the practice of the subtle thread pride themselves on returning to the source as the ultimate Way. Yet they fail to realize that when one contemplates the mind through the four aggregates, the mind cannot be apprehended;

when one contemplates the body through the four elements, the body cannot be apprehended. Since both body and mind cannot be apprehended, the ocean of awakening becomes limpid and perfect, pervading all of space.
Pervading the entire realm, how could one deign to mistake it for a floating bubble or distance it from the vast ocean? It is clear, therefore, that existence must not be clung to.
To cling to emptiness—claiming that after death there is annihilation and no saṃsāra, and that both good and evil, the wise and the foolish, have no retribution in future lives—is a great false view;
it is not even worth discussing. Such is the reckless Zen of those who, in their vacuity, falsely claim that purity and defilement are one and the same. Eastward...

There is no separation from the West; entrust yourself to the natural flow of things—what need is there for seeking? Little do you realize that while ignorance remains unbroken, the seeds of karma are still very much present.
To speak of emptiness at every turn only serves to increase one’s pride. When obscured by the transition between lives, one loses the ability to govern oneself;

the retributions of the three miserable realms must then be experienced by oneself. Thus, it is clear that emptiness is not something to be grasped. Only when these two attachments are broken does one [attain liberation].
Being able to accord with the Buddha’s words, they shall give rise to the great bodhicitta and be born together with these sentient beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Third, regarding the explanation of the section on the main teaching (*samyak-artha-bhāga*): from the moment the World-Honored One emitted light from between his eyebrows until all the devas resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path, this is called the section on the main teaching.

The World-Honored One emitted light from between his eyebrows, manifesting various pure lands, and caused Vaidehī herself— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the partial nature of the source.*
As for "selection," it is because among all Buddha-lands, none surpasses the Land of Ultimate Bliss in its purity and radiance;
seeing this with one's own physical eyes, one’s faith and delight deepen manifold. From this contemplation, one immediately attains right concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding the subsequent passage which will clarify the Pure Contemplation, the instruction first given to sentient beings to cultivate the three types of merit is because, through worldly dharmas, one gradually reaches the supramundane dharma—just as when storing clarified butter (*sarpis*), one first [prepares the vessel].
One must purify one’s vessel; if the vessel is impure, its contents will be spoiled.

Those who practice filial piety and support their parents recognize that sentient beings possess their bodies by depending upon their parents, and it is by depending upon this body that they know there is a Buddha.
Therefore, if one does not respect one’s own body, one cannot achieve all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); if one does not respect one’s parents, one cannot cultivate and increase all merit.
Tian said: "Some claim that when the Tathāgata abandoned his kin to leave the household life, they suspect this violates the principle of filial piety and nourishment.

They fail to realize that there is worldly filial piety and there is supramundane filial piety. Worldly filial piety consists in providing full support while one's parents are alive and offering full sacrifices after their death;

once one has established oneself in conduct and made one's name renowned to future generations, that is sufficient. Supramundane filial piety, however, necessarily requires that one's own kin transcend the three realms of existence."
Realizing non-arising, the way of the son is finally perfected; in filial piety toward one's parents, who can surpass this?
Regarding the service of teachers and elders, there are those who are worldly teachers and elders, and there are those who are supramundane teachers and elders.

Those who guide one with the studies of poetry and the classics, and urge one along the path of benevolence and righteousness, are worldly teachers and elders. Those who enlighten one with the teachings of the Three Honored Ones and advance one [therein]...
The Gate of Non-duality is the teacher who transcends the world; it is fitting that one should serve it with single-minded devotion.

To possess a heart of compassion and refrain from killing is the very mind of the Buddha, for great kindness and compassion are its essence. Among the evil karmas of this Sahā world, none exceeds the taking of life; through it, one incurs the enmity of countless kalpas.

It arises from killing. When the intent to kill is not severed, then the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is not fulfilled. When the mind of loving-kindness is not fulfilled, one stands in opposition and duality with all sentient beings.
To stand in opposition and duality with all sentient beings is to stand in opposition and duality with the Tathāgata.

It is difficult to seek birth in the Pure Land. Regarding the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala*): these consist of the three mental actions, the three physical actions, and the four verbal actions.

If one can cultivate the ten wholesome actions to counteract the ten unwholesome actions, then past obstructions will gradually be eliminated. Once past obstructions have been eliminated, rebirth there will be without hindrance.
However, it is essential to receive the Three Refuges and expand upon them with the various precepts; for if one does not receive the Three Refuges, then [one cannot proceed].
One can plant the seeds for transcendence; yet, if one does not possess the various precepts, one cannot cultivate the foundation for transcendence.

This is because taking the Three Refuges and observing the various precepts constitutes the correct cause for entering the Buddha-way. Nevertheless, even if one is fully endowed with the Refuges and Precepts, if one does not resolve to attain Bodhicitta, then despite having abundant merit, it will ultimately remain tainted (*sāsrava*).
This is because such merit does not accord with the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Non-reliant Wisdom. Why?
This is called "generating the bodhicitta. *Bodhi* means awakening. It is the thorough knowledge that the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are without self and without what belongs to a self.
Based upon the *dharmadhātu*, one gives rise to aspiration and seeking; it is as vast and penetrating as empty space, equal and compliant.

Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are perfectly integrated in a single thought-moment, with no further distinction, as described in the "Chapter on the Merit of First Generating the Mind" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

One who gives rise to such a mind will swiftly attain Buddhahood. Those who have deep faith in cause and effect understand that performing good brings blessings, while performing evil brings calamity.

It is like how ginseng primarily functions to supplement vitality, while rhubarb primarily functions to purge; whether one is supplemented or purged depends entirely on what is inherently present within the person.

Thus we know that performing good is itself blessing—there is no blessing apart from good—and performing evil is itself calamity—there is no calamity apart from evil. This is what is meant by "cause and effect."
At the same time, it is thus: a single thought-moment of reciting the Buddha’s name is itself the Buddha; every successive thought-moment of recollecting the Buddha is nothing but the Buddha.
When the mind is pure, the land is pure—it is likewise so. Those who read and recite the Mahāyāna, if they do not read the Mahāyāna, will not understand the Buddha’s mind.

If they do not understand the Buddha’s mind, they will not accord with the Buddha’s wisdom. If they do not accord with the Buddha’s wisdom, even if they are born in that land, they will not [attain liberation].

One attains the vision of the Buddha; the fruit clarifies the Buddha-mind, and the fruit accords with Buddha-wisdom. For the sake of benefiting oneself and others, the impulse is such that it cannot be suppressed, for the Buddha and sentient beings are of one and the same essence.
One practices the three types of merit in equal measure, fulfilling the pure causes. Whether through contemplation or recitation, one proceeds accordingly.
Whatever one seeks according to one's vows, it is like holding a mirror to capture an image or raising one's voice to elicit an echo; how could there be any distance?
The Sūtra employs the contemplation of the name of Amitāyus Buddha not by directing one immediately to visualize the Buddha, but first by means of the setting sun.
This is because the sun is near and easy to see, because it allows for firm concentration and right orientation, and because its radiance is so penetrating that it shatters the darkness.
First, darkness; because one sees the Buddha’s stairway, next comes ice, then earth, then trees, then water, and finally the various jewels and so forth.

The Buddha’s contemplation is profound and subtle, such that it cannot be entered by the coarse perceptions of sentient beings. First, he contemplates the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment as retribution), thereby purifying and eliminating defiled attachments.
Once this single contemplation is accomplished, the remaining contemplations will also be easy. For earth, water, fire, and wind each and every one possesses the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
how much more so the pure vows and adornments of Amitābha Buddha? Not a single speck of dust nor a single sound is not a place where our Buddha manifests his body and preaches the Dharma.

All visualizations proceed from the coarse to the subtle and thus belong to the gradual approach (*anupūrvika-mārga*). When contemplating the Buddha’s body, one first uses the flower seat to gradually draw near and become intimate, before finally entering the fundamental position.
In essence, this sutra takes the visualization of the Buddha as primary, with the other visualizations serving as auxiliaries.

Within the visualization of the Buddha, the provisional vehicles (*upāya-yāna*) are subsumed and fully returned to the single reality (*ekārtha*). Therefore, it is said: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*)."

Entering into the thoughts within the minds of all sentient beings, this mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Tathāgatas’ correct and universal knowledge arises from the thoughts of the mind.

One who enters this contemplation does not traverse a gradual path, yet is fully adorned; this is called the Sudden Gate (*tongo*). "That which acts" is free from the meaning of spontaneity (*jinen*);

"that which is" is free from the meaning of causes and conditions (*innen*). To know that this mind creates the Buddha—[one does not... (Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
To know that this mind is the Buddha is to obscure the fundamental wondrousness and become stagnant in one's meritorious achievements.

To know that this mind is the Buddha, yet not know that this mind makes the Buddha, is to follow natural spontaneity while neglecting cultivation and realization. Departing from these two extremes, a single thought is perfectly integrated.
This clarifies the Middle Way, which is also termed the "One Mind and Three Contemplations. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Whatever has marks is entirely illusory.
If one perceives all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. This clarifies the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
[The Buddha] said: "Do not harbor this thought: 'The Tathāgata attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of fully endowed marks.'"
This clarifies the contemplation of the provisional (jia-guan). The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata is, within it, neither real nor false;

this clarifies the contemplation of the middle (zhong-guan). Thus, the water-birds, the forest trees, the jewel ponds, and the pearl nets—whether form or non-form, sound or non-sound—are all in their entirety True Suchness (*tathatā*), like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, or a shadow. Therefore, it is said: "To give rise to *anuttara*..."

[They] arouse the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Regarding all phenomena, he does not speak of their mark of annihilation. Sentient beings rely upon the mind and its objects to perceive the Buddha-body;
this is the Buddha of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), not the ultimate Buddha. However, without contemplative practice, the ultimate would not be manifested.

It is through contemplative practice that one attains the ultimate, and only then is one called the Truly and Fully Enlightened One (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). Because one contemplates the Buddha-body, one also perceives [it].
The Buddha-mind knows that the body is not different from the mind; therefore, its adornments are not existent. The Buddha-mind knows that the mind is not different from the body;
therefore, its profound stillness is not non-existent. The Buddha-mind is great compassion. It gathers in all sentient beings through unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*).
Because it is unconditioned, there is nothing it does not encompass, and nothing it does not reach. Yet, this compassion is without form; though it is manifest, it cannot be seen.
There is nothing more luminous than this. Ordinary beings possess eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), which the Buddhas transform into eighty-four thousand *pāramitā* dharma-gates.
Thus, each mark (*lakṣaṇa*), each secondary sign (*anuvyañjana*), and each ray of light is fully endowed with the number eighty-four thousand.
These rays shine universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions upon sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, gathering them in and protecting them.
[The Buddha] replied: "Disciples, you should know that sentient beings, in every single thought-moment, are constantly within the light of my Buddha’s great compassion.

Whether sitting, lying down, or walking, they are separated from it by not even a hair’s breadth. Among all these lights, the light of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows) is the foremost.
Those who contemplate this white tuft do so with an inconceivable mind, taking an inconceivable object as their focus. You should know that this light is both form and mind."

It is neither mind nor form; it comes from nowhere, nor does it go anywhere. Upon entering this light, the eighty-four thousand marks and signs appear vividly and simultaneously, without deficiency or excess.

The Buddhas of the ten directions all manifest clearly. Question: Since the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are not the ultimate reality but are merely manifestations of one's own mind, why not directly contemplate one’s own Buddha instead of intentionally causing [the practitioner] to circumambulate them? Answer: Because the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*...
That which is not true [regards] the Dharmakāya as having something external to it. Does the Dharmakāya truly have anything external?

Knowing that the Dharmakāya has nothing external, one is thus able to penetrate the Dharmakāya through the Nirmāṇakāya and Saṃbhogakāya. The Dharmakāya is neither born nor extinguished; it is neither identical nor different.

The Nirmāṇakāya and Saṃbhogakāya are likewise neither born nor extinguished; they are neither identical nor different. Those who perceive them as subject to birth and extinction, or as being identical or different, [are mistaken].
This is merely the measure of the emotional capacity of sentient beings. When this emotional capacity is exhausted, one encounters the manifest reality directly.
Within every single mark, within every single minor characteristic, and within every single ray of light, the boundless great ocean of quiescent extinction is fully present.

If one does not enter this gate, it cannot be called the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance. Question: Since all meditative visualizations are complete with the three contemplations, are they real and not provisional? Are they sudden?
It is not gradual. Why? Because within the absence of identity or difference, there is still the distinction between the provisional and the real, and between the sudden and the gradual.

Answer: In reality, there is no dharma distinct from the Dharma; however, there are degrees of depth in realization. Since the sutra is titled "Contemplating the Buddha," one must naturally take the contemplation of the Buddha as the primary practice.

When the contemplation of the Buddha is perfected, one directly beholds all Buddhas of the ten directions; only then is it called the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi), and one is born before all Buddhas.

One realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). Because one has profoundly penetrated the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one is thus able to immediately realize non-arising.

Those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, suddenly comprehend that all is but mind; they proceed directly without obstruction and need not further cultivate other contemplations.
As stated in the *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa-sūtra*: "However, these various contemplations possess distinct stages. When the contemplation of ice is perfected..."
When the visualization of water is perfected, one hears the sounds of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.

When the visualization of the Buddha is perfected, one hears the praise of the Buddha’s marks and signs, as well as the sounds of mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration, one constantly hears the sublime Dharma, which accords with the Sūtras.
By advancing from the Small Vehicle to the Great, what is realized is roughly the same as that of the superior and middling classes mentioned later. As for their rebirth...

The grades [of rebirth] may likewise be inferred by analogy. The practitioner should personally assess their own faculties and capacity—whether they are of one grade, several combined, or fully endowed with the contemplations—but must take certain rebirth in the Pure Land as the sole standard;
thus, there will be no mistaken path. Prior to Zhiyi, the first thirteen contemplations were divided among the nine grades, but this was not yet a definitive doctrine.
Once the first contemplation is accomplished, it already belongs to the realm of established fact (*shiding*), which corresponds to the middle grade; how much more so for the subsequent ones?
In the second and third [stages], the pure contemplation gradually deepens, until one barely attains the upper or middle grades of the lower level.
Having already contemplated the body of the Buddha, one then contemplates Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta; these two bodhisattvas, together with Amitāyus Buddha, [constitute the assembly].

The principal and the attendants intermingle; their emanations pervade the dust-like lands of the cosmos, collectively performing Buddha-work through radiance to gather in sentient beings and lead them all back to the Pure Land.

One must know that when a sentient being recites the Buddha’s name for even a single thought-moment and realizes that the essence of this mindfulness is fundamentally empty, they are named Avalokiteśvara.
When a sentient being recites the Buddha’s name for even a single thought-moment and has faith that the power of this mindfulness is fully perfected, they are named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Knowing that the essence of thought is fundamentally empty, one thinks yet is without thought. Knowing that the power of thought is fully endowed, one arises from non-arising.
Without thought, there is thought; the essence of thought is all-pervasive. Arising, there is no arising; the principle of arising is eternally quiescent. Thus it is one and three simultaneously.
Neither three nor one—this is named Amitāyus Buddha.
The preceding passage has already clarified that Amitāyus Buddha is fully endowed with physical marks;

yet, the instruction to visualize the Buddha’s body as sixteen feet tall is a skillful means established according to the mental capacity of ordinary beings. When this visualization is perfected, one will gradually come to see the Buddha.
Possessing the marks of a perfect body, as described in the *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa-sūtra*, one should be instructed to go to a vihāra and contemplate the image of the Buddha.
Sitting upright in meditation for twenty-one days, one will immediately see the Tathāgata appearing before one, emitting light and preaching the Dharma.
One should contemplate that the Buddha is produced by one's own mind; apart from the mind, there is no Buddha. This extends even to the three periods of time being one.
It is the same for all Buddhas; they are likewise entirely non-existent, existing only in reliance upon one’s own mind.

Therefore, this sutra may manifest a large body or a small body, according to the minds of sentient beings and in accordance with the capacity of their understanding. Like the moon in water or flowers in a mirror, it is neither empty nor real.
Regarding "birth in the highest grade," it requires that one be fully endowed with the three minds: namely, the mind of utmost sincerity, the profound mind, and the mind of dedication and aspiration.
To possess these three minds is called the arousal of the bodhicitta. What is meant by "utmost sincerity"? "Utmost" (*zhi*) means leaving no room for anything else;
"sincerity" (*cheng*) means having only this single mind. When the practitioner first hears that "this very mind creates the Buddha" and "this very mind is the Buddha," [they realize this].

This is the meaning. To give rise to the mind of Śāntarakṣita and Huiyuan, one should proceed directly toward unsurpassed bodhi, no longer aspiring for the remaining nirvāṇa or the karmic rewards of humans and devas.
One should simply reflect that if one does not rely on the power of the Buddha, it will be difficult to fulfill one's practices and vows;

therefore, one must resolutely seek rebirth in the Pure Land. To cultivate with single-minded diligence without interruption—this is called "sincerity. What is meant by "profound mind"? As the Sūtra says:
With a profound mind of faith and understanding, one is ever pure. The extremely profound Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas cannot be understood through conceptualization or discrimination;
yet, it is not separate from the deluded thoughts within the minds of sentient beings. Therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This wisdom of the Tathāgata is none other than the deluded thoughts of sentient beings, and those deluded thoughts are nothing other than this.
Furthermore, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is such that it is illuminated and realized solely through the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*).

Knowing that the Tathāgata and sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction, one does not perceive the Buddha outside of the mind; for the Buddha perceived does not depart from one’s own mind.

Knowing that the Tathāgata and sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction, one does not seek birth in a Pure Land outside of the mind, realizing that which is born [is none other than the mind itself].
The Pure Land is so called because it is fully endowed with one’s own mind. Even to the point that seeing is itself non-seeing and birth is itself non-birth;

it is primordially pure because it is free from all discursive thought and observation (*vitarka-vicāra*). To have such faith and understanding is what is called the "profound mind" (*adhyāśaya*). What is meant by the "mind of dedication and aspiration"?
It is as when Amitābha Buddha, for the sake of the Buddha-way, gave rise to a vast and great mind; I, too, shall likewise do so for the sake of Buddhahood.

For this reason, I have resolved to develop the vast and great mind. Just as Amitābha Buddha, for the sake of sentient beings, took up a pure and wondrous land, so too shall I, for the sake of sentient beings, take up a pure and wondrous land.

As long as there is even a single sentient being who has not yet attained liberation, my land shall not be pure, and my Buddhahood shall not be realized. My Buddha and sentient beings are one and three, yet neither three nor [not-three].

First, because it is ultimately unattainable, this is called the mind of dedication and aspiration. These three minds also possess the three truths: the first is the contemplation of emerging from emptiness into the provisional;

the second is the contemplation of returning from the provisional back to emptiness; and the third is the contemplation of simultaneous cessation and illumination within a single thought-moment of perfect fusion.
Regarding the "three kinds of sentient beings," this refers to sentient beings who practice these three types of activities together; it does not [refer to...].

This means that each [of the six] practices one kind [of recollection]. Generally, faith and aspiration support one another, while understanding and practice stimulate one another; if even one of these is deficient, one cannot enter the Path.

The "Six Recollections" refer to the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, Generosity, Precepts, and Devas. For one who possesses these merits, speaking in terms of a long duration, it may last from one day up to seven days.
According to both the *Shorter Text* on the holding of the Name and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* on the binding of mindfulness, all of these [practices] are present.

The text states that the Sūtra specifically emphasizes these points: one must strive for single-mindedness without distraction and achieve results within a fixed period; this constitutes "vigorous and courageous" practice.

Zhiyi (Sishiming) maintains that whether [the faculties] are complete or partial, they may all be said to be "endowed. Regarding the high or low grade of rebirth, this is determined by the degree of abandonment and subduing (*prahāṇa-vibhava*), as well as whether [the defilements] have been entirely unsubdued.
However, the merit of abandonment and subduing must arise through gradual accumulation; thus, the three types of faculties cannot be fully perfected at once.
It is difficult to expect such a supreme fruit. By emerging from the state of distraction and entering meditative concentration, one penetrates the single mind and only then achieves samādhi.
Because their preceptual conduct is fully perfected, they perceive the physical forms of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in their complete splendor.

Because they have faith and joy in the Mahāyāna, upon hearing the preaching of the wondrous Dharma, they immediately attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Having received their prediction (vyākaraṇa), they immediately obtain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇīs.

Section on the Gate. Those of the middle birth in the highest grade have already attained an awakening to the primary truth (*paramārtha*), yet their merit in cultivation and realization is inferior to that of those born in the highest grade;
therefore, their birth rank is next. Those of the lower birth in the highest grade give rise to the mind for the unsurpassed path.

Their dedication and vows transcend those of the two vehicles, being the same as those of the two preceding groups; however, because their practice and understanding are not yet fully perfected, their stage of birth is ranked next.
The "Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha) is the true mark of all phenomena (dharmas), free from the four extremes and transcending the hundred negations;
it can only be known through direct realization and cannot be fathomed by the mundane mind. It is like when the Buddha was in the Jeta Grove preaching the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where all...
The great śrāvakas neither heard nor saw this. At the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there were also bhikṣus who withdrew from their seats;

thus we know that this matter is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. Question: Between reciting and explaining the meaning, one should naturally regard explaining the meaning as superior and reciting as inferior.
Why is it that reciting is instead ranked as leading to rebirth in the higher realms, while explaining the meaning takes the secondary place? Answer: This reciting... [text continues]
Recite while simultaneously comprehending the meaning. If one does not understand the primary meaning, how could one fully possess the three minds?

By understanding the meaning while concurrently engaging in recitation, one employs inconceivable perfuming to enter non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). The dharma-realm unfolds in successive layers, entirely returning to one's own nature;
the lands of the ten directions are not separated by even the tip of a hair. Among all auxiliary conditions, none surpasses this for attaining the highest realization.

The patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) corresponds to the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*) and the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This is the fruit of further progress attained after this life;

however, according to the perspective of what is presently manifest, it belongs to the various stages prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching. Therefore, Tiantai classifies it as the "nature of the path-seeds" (*mārgajñatā-gotra*).

The upper-middle [levels] constitute the nature-seed (prakṛti-bīja), while the upper-lower constitute the cultivation-seed (paripuṣṭa-bīja); these correspond to the ten dedications, the ten practices, and the ten abidings.

To judge the middle three grades as being below the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā) likely does not reflect the intent of the sūtra, for the ten stages of faith are the foremost of the three levels of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Having established the foundation of the Mahāyāna and been born in that land, they have heard the Dharma and progressed; they should together attain the first stage (Prathamabhūmi).

There is absolutely no principle by which they would regress to realize the Hīnayāna. If it is claimed that these are Śrāvakas who have regressed from Bodhicitta, then having regressed from Bodhicitta, they have already departed from the stage of faith (Śraddhābhūmi).
How can one falsely assume this title? I, a fool, privately consider that within the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one should correspond to the lower or middle levels. The Sūtra states:

"Merely having resolved upon the unsurpassed Way, while the perfect understanding has not yet opened"—this precisely coincides with the stage of Faith, wherein one relies on the four immeasurable truths to give rise to the Four Great Vows.

The upper-middle level should correspond to the first *vihāra* (abode) and above; once born there, one immediately severs the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) and attains [the fruit].

The stage of regression corresponds to the seventh dwelling (*bhūmi*). The successive higher stages correspond to the eighth dwelling through the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). Having already severed the dust-like afflictions (*rajas*), only ignorance (*avidyā*) remains unbroken.
Upon hearing the Dharma, one advances and suddenly shatters ignorance; therefore, this is called attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The five grades of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) correspond in rank to the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). The grade of "Birth" can be understood accordingly. As for those who attain rebirth through these very grades according to Tiantai, how could it be...?
Regarding the three grades of the superior category, the lower grade is that of the heterodox.
In the superior grade, both the vehicle (*yāna*) and the precepts (*śīla*) are urgent. In the middling-superior grade, the precepts are urgent while the vehicle is lax. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:

"When sentient beings receive the Buddha's precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas. The Buddhas have no substance; the Dharma is their substance. The Buddhas have no marks; the precepts are their marks."
This is the manifestation of the sign. Therefore, those sentient beings who uphold the Buddha’s precepts will connect with the Tathāgata’s flow of Dharma.

Although the period—midday for one day and one night—is brief, because the power of their faith is already deep and they have been perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far off.

Those of middle and lower capacities have few pure causes from the past, yet their roots of goodness have already matured; thus, upon receiving a single instruction, they are transformed like rain falling from the heavens.

Among these three grades, the former grade is characterized by a profound weariness with birth and death, and, relying on the Four Noble Truths of the Tripitaka teachings, they give rise to the supramundane mind.
They cultivate and accumulate the roots of goodness and dedicate them toward rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Upon hearing the Dharma, their practice advances;

as the afflictions of view and thought are exhausted, they realize the four fruits of the path. Regarding the latter two classes: one has briefly touched upon the categories of precepts, while the other practices only mundane virtues.

By dedicating their karma for human and celestial realms toward rebirth, and through hearing the Dharma, their afflictions of view are first exhausted, and they attain the first fruit. Such individuals as these are [the subjects of] the Buddha’s...
Through the compassionate empowerment [of the Buddha], they are further able to turn back from the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle and do not abide in the provisional vehicles.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "All these people shall attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
In the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, those of the three grades who attain rebirth all resolve for Bodhicitta, with the exception of those who have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the Dharma.
There is, however, a separate class known as "womb-birth" (garbhaja), which exists because they harbor doubts regarding the Buddha’s wisdom. Indeed, the Bodhicitta does not arise without wisdom;

thus, this sūtra applies only to the three superior grades, which roughly correspond to the three grades of the *Mahāvaipulya*. As for the middle grade, they seek only their own benefit; even if they do not...
To give rise to doubt is essentially to fail to understand the Buddha’s wisdom; therefore, one remains in the interval between the womb and transformation.

From the lower grade of the lowest level who later turn their minds, dwelling within the lotus-womb from the seventh week onward until twelve great kalpas, all are subsumed under the "womb-birth" of the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sukhāvatīvyūha] Sūtra.
Tiantai takes the nine grades of this sūtra to correspond to the three classes of the *Mahāvaipulya*; one should know that this is not the case.

Those three classes of beings are all born by transformation (*upapāduka*). As for those born from a womb, they have never failed to believe in sin and merit, nor have they failed to cultivate the roots of goodness;
yet, because they do not believe in the Buddha’s wisdom, they still fall into the City of Doubt. Those of the lowest grade in this sutra have already accumulated grave evils to maturity;

even if they were not to be born in the City of Doubt, they would certainly dwell in the borderlands, remaining very far removed from those who are born by transformation. Thus, regarding the five heinous crimes and the slandering [of the Dharma]...

Regarding the *Dharmakara Sūtra* (the "Original Text"), those who do not belong to the three grades are excluded because it seeks to distinguish [this teaching] from birth from a womb (*jarāyu-jāti*). This sūtra includes them because it does not discard the possibility of womb-birth.
By using this criterion to distinguish between the two sūtras, there is no longer any contradiction. Furthermore, Tiantai stated that practice consists of both the distracted and the concentrated;

since the *Original Text* discusses distracted goodness, it says that those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the Dharma cannot attain rebirth. This sūtra, however, clarifies meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Therefore, it is said that one attains birth [in the Pure Land]. Yet this is not so. Only when the pure contemplation (*śubhā-vipaśyanā*) is perfected is it called "concentrated goodness" (*samādhi-kuśala*).

As for merely reciting the Buddha’s name during the final stage of life, provided it is complete with ten recitations—how does this differ from the ten recitations of the *Mahāyāna-sukhāvatī-vyūha* Sūtra?

To insist on distinguishing between "concentrated" and "scattered" states is something I personally find incomprehensible. As for those of such a kind who attain birth, it depends upon the individual first giving rise to faith; even a single thought-moment...
Turning the light back, with courageous and diligent effort, one becomes no different from those who have long practiced.

This is because the Dharma-body of all Buddhas neither increases when in the state of a sage nor decreases when among ordinary beings; it is only through the power of conditions and causes that it is manifested.

As previously stated, once the contemplation of the earth is accomplished, one eliminates the offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death; yet, regarding the final two stages, one merely hears of Amitābha...
Through the majestic power of the Ten Powers of the Tathāgata, and by invoking the Buddha’s name while maintaining the ten recitations, one's offenses are extinguished and merit is produced;

this is identical to that [previous] example. Thus we know that time has no duration—neither long nor short—and practice has no degree—neither shallow nor deep. Provided one attains firm and steadfast right mindfulness, the accomplishment of the goal will be achieved with certainty at the mere turn of a finger.
For those of the lowest grade among men, it is essential to take faith in the existence of offense and merit as the cause; therefore, they ultimately attain the fruit of their transgressions.
This is the fruit produced by the extinction of merit. If one does not believe in this, how could one possibly be born even in the borderlands of the City of Doubt?
Question: Prior to the thirteen contemplations, all clarify the methods of contemplation; yet, regarding the nine grades of rebirth, these do not extend to such contemplations.

"Must those who are reborn there necessarily practice *vipaśyanā* (contemplation)? Or is it not always so? Answer: "There is a distinction between exclusive cultivation (*senju*) and combined cultivation (*kenshu*).
Prior to the thirteen contemplations, there is mostly exclusive cultivation; among the nine grades [of rebirth], there is mostly combined cultivation.

Regarding the dedication of merit and the aspiration for rebirth, whether for one day up to seven days, contemplation is included therein. As for the high or low grade of the rebirth attained, one must observe..."

The breadth or narrowness of one’s resolve, and the depth or shallowness of one’s understanding and practice, do not depend entirely on whether one is single-mindedly devoted or engages in both [exclusive and inclusive practices].

However, if one wishes to see the Buddha in this very life, then exclusive cultivation is superior. For instance, when the ninth visualization is accomplished, one attains the vision of immeasurable Buddhas appearing before one to bestow predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
This is further distinguished from the "uppermost grade of upper birth," which necessarily awaits the bestowal of a prediction after one has been reborn.
Progressing further, the single practice of holding the Name is likewise so. If one does not keep this in mind with constant mindfulness, how can one attain a single-mindedness free from distraction?
Once single-mindedness is attained, it is not difficult to see the Buddha. As for the text concerning the nine grades, they are collectively termed "contemplation" (guan).

In order to cause the practitioner to possess the wisdom of discernment, to arouse the mind of diligence, to abandon the low and hasten toward the high, and to turn away from the small and head toward the great, one first causes them to know that they are sustained by the power of the Tathāgata’s vows, such that no one lacking the capacity is excluded. Question: Regarding the "prediction conferred in the presence":
Since they have already transcended and been born above, they are at the highest level of the nine grades. Is there yet another grade? Answer:

The previous text stated that by relinquishing the body in another world, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), which is precisely equivalent to being born above. From this point onward, one progressively realizes the three bodies (*trikāya*).
He travels unimpeded to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; he cannot be categorized among the nine grades. Question:

When those of the lower grade have their flowers open, they immediately give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Why is this considered superior to those of the middle grade who merely realize the stage of a *śrāvaka*? Answer:

This is because, at the moment of death, they fear transgression and thus give rise to a courageous and resolute mind. Furthermore, having remained within the flower-womb for a long time, it is as if they are wandering through a land of fragrance.

Because their bodies possess a fragrant scent. Furthermore, it is not that virtuous people alone possess dull faculties; there are also those among the wicked who possess sharp faculties and believe immediately upon hearing [the teaching].
Because their faculties are sharp, they merely realize the stage of a Śrāvaka. Because their faculties are dull, although they have aspirations, these are not urgent.

Thus, even if those of inferior grade give rise to the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), the realization of the fruit remains far off; as for those of middling grade who have already realized the stage of a Śrāvaka, they merely...

They resolve upon the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment and receive a prediction of future buddhahood in the present life, just as Śāriputra and others did at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

There is no doubt that they will attain Buddhahood; thus we know that there is originally no fixed status between the Great and Small Vehicles, and the sūtras merely cite these as representative examples. Question:

Question: May the inhabitants of the city of doubt also participate in the nine grades? Answer: Provided they give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), they will not be far from the Buddha and shall participate in the nine grades.

As stated in the *Mūla-sūtra*: "If these sentient beings recognize their fundamental transgressions, deeply repent and reproach themselves, and seek to leave that place, they will immediately attain their wish and proceed to the abode of Amitāyus Buddha, where they will pay homage and make offerings. This refers to such individuals.

If one does not resolve to attain the Way, there will be no opportunity to see the Buddha, and it will be difficult to expect entry into the ranks of the sages. This is because those of the lower grade all resolve to attain the Way, a state that cannot be reached by those who are indolent or arrogant.
Although this sutra belongs to the gradual gate, it also encompasses the sudden teaching; although it clarifies the provisional vehicles, it especially prizes perfect cultivation.
For instance, the "Chapter on Contemplating the Buddha" directly points to the essence of the mind, and the "Chapter on the Superior Class" repeatedly mentions the Mahāyāna.

Therefore, those who hear it may attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) or give rise to the mind of supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*); all of this is due to the inconceivable merit of this sutra.

Discourse: The majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) bestowed by Amitābha Buddha is likewise inconceivable. Question: Tiantai regarded this sutra as *sudden* (*dun*), whereas you now consider it *gradual* (*jian*). Why is this? Answer: If we discuss this in terms of the ritual of transformation (*huayi*), only the *Avataṃsaka* belongs to the sudden; all others belong to the gradual. This sutra is subsumed under the Vaipulya (*fangdeng*) category; thus, it is gradual and not sudden. Furthermore, among the various sutras, while some exclusively discourse upon the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), this one does not. Therefore, it is classified as gradual. Moreover, although the *Lotus Sutra* is considered sudden, its primary purpose is to lead those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). This sutra, however, is for the sake of those who have already entered the Great Vehicle, enabling them to attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). Consequently, it is categorized as gradual. Furthermore, the *Lotus Sutra* is a teaching of the final period (*paścimakāla*), whereas this sutra is a teaching of the intermediate period. For these reasons, it is designated as gradual. Finally, regarding the title: the term "Amitābha" is a name that encompasses both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). The term "Sukhāvatīvyūha" refers to the adornment of the land, which is the manifestation of phenomena based on principle. Because it explains both principle and phenomena, it is called the *Amitābha Sutra*. It is not like the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, which is titled after a specific person, nor the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, which is titled after a specific meditative state, nor the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, which is titled after a specific practice. Thus, it is called the *Amitābha Sutra*. As for the term "Sutra," it means "to string together" (*sūtraṇa*). Just as a garland-maker strings flowers together, so too does the Buddha string together the teachings of the Dharma to form a single volume. Hence, it is called a "sutra. As for "Vol. 1," it indicates the first part of the work. This concludes the preface. Now, let us enter the main text. [The text continues with the formal opening of the scripture. At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, in the palace adorned with the seven treasures, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. At that moment, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having received the Buddha’s majestic empowerment, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One, I wish to ask about a matter. May the Tathāgata, out of compassion, grant me the opportunity to speak. The Buddha said to Avalokiteśvara: "You may ask whatever you desire. I shall explain it for you. Then the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings in the lands of the ten directions who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and, having heard it, give rise to a mind of pure faith and joy, and at the time of their death, if they are able to see the Buddha and his retinue, and if they do not fall back into the three evil realms, how many kalpas must they cultivate before they can be born in that land? The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara: "If there are sentient beings in the lands of the ten directions who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and, having heard it, give rise to a mind of pure faith and joy, and at the time of their death, if they are able to see the Buddha and his retinue, and if they do not fall back into the three evil realms, they will be born in that land after cultivating for ten thousand kalpas. Avalokiteśvara asked: "World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and, having heard it, give rise to a mind of pure faith and joy, and at the time of their death, if they are able to see the Buddha and his retinue, and if they do not fall back into the three evil realms, but are unable to see the Buddha and his retinue, how many kalpas must they cultivate before they can be born in that land? The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara: "If there are sentient beings who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and, having heard it, give rise to a mind of pure faith and joy, and at the time of their death, if they are unable to see the Buddha and his retinue, and they fall back into the three evil realms, they will be born in that land after cultivating for thirty thousand kalpas. Avalokiteśvara asked: "World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and, having heard it, give rise to a mind of pure faith and joy, and at the time of their death, if they are unable to see the Buddha and his retinue, and they fall back into the three evil realms, and furthermore, if they do not encounter a good friend to guide them, how many kalpas must they cultivate before they can be born in that land? The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara: "If there are sentient beings who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and, having heard it, give rise to a mind of pure faith and joy, and at the time of their death, if they are unable to see the Buddha and his retinue, and they fall back into the three evil realms, and furthermore, if they do not encounter a good friend to guide them, they will be born in that land after cultivating for forty thousand kalpas. Avalokiteśvara asked: "World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and, having heard it, give rise to a mind of pure faith and joy, and at the time of their death, if they are unable to see the Buddha and his retinue, and they fall back into the three evil realms, and furthermore, if they do not encounter a good friend to guide them, and they do not even hear the name of Amitābha Buddha again, how many kalpas must they cultivate before they can be born in that land? The sudden [teaching] is the direct approach; applying skillful means in a circuitous manner constitutes the gradual. The gradual belongs to the provisional (upāya), while the sudden is termed the real (bhūta).

Yet within the gradual there is the sudden, and within the provisional there is the real. It is simply that by realizing the one mind, no other dharma exists. This is the profound intent behind Tiantai’s judgment.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the *parīndanā* (concluding) section: from "At that time, Ānanda" until "paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew" is called the *parīndanā* section.
While the sutra names this [practice] "contemplation" (*guan*), the merit of upholding the name (*ming*) in the lower grade is equal to that of practicing contemplation;

furthermore, in the *parīndanā* section, the merit of hearing the name is praised again. This is because contemplation arises from the mind, whereas the name originates from the Buddha; by means of contemplation, one gathers the mind, and [the name] is entirely...
The mind is Buddha. One invokes Buddha by its name; the Buddha is entirely the mind. To know directly where one returns, they are neither one nor different.
With one’s whole body, one presses into it; there is nothing lacking and nothing remaining.
